en: In the preface to the *Recorded Sayings* of the Great Master Rujing, Shouchang remarked that while the lineage of descendants from the ancient virtuous elder Muzhou was sparse, he foresaw that Linji would provide shade for the future and Yunmen would stimulate it with his penetrating brilliance.
Although Linji succeeded Huangbo and Yunmen succeeded... [text fragment] ...Yunmen.
Xuefeng’s hand-eye for seizing the opportune moment and his opening move indeed surpassed those of Muzhou;
ultimately, the descendants of both lineages became part of his dharma lineage. Yet, Muzhou did not accept that title. Such was his mode of action.
How could it be merely that a colt tramples others to death while possessing the air of a king?

I have often recklessly reflected upon our Master, who opened the source for a thousand ages and encompassed the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human). Yet, whenever people were unaware of his virtue, he never suffered from resentment;

this is stated repeatedly throughout the entire Analects. What is the meaning of this? It is because when one examines the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, as soon as they open their mouths—

Recently, upon hearing the single word "no" (bu), my countenance immediately changed. Thus, among the eminent scholars of the School of Principle (Lixue) who pursue fame and achievement, those who follow Zhu Xi and those who follow Lu Jiuyuan dispute over differences;

though they share the same ancestral tradition, they divide into factions, often becoming mortal enemies. It is evident that this single thought of seeking knowledge has come along with innate ignorance (sahaja-avidyā).
Even if various external conditions are gradually eliminated, this thought of resentment and affliction is difficult to forget all at once. As the ancients said:

Laozi and Zhuangzi could not avoid being "existent"; therefore, they constantly instructed people using the term "non-being" (*wu*). It can be seen that Confucius could not avoid possessing "knowledge";
therefore, he repeatedly instructed people by saying, "Do not worry about not being respected. As for his sigh of "no words and no one knows," this final word was immediately attributed to Heaven.
Yet, upon meeting Laozi once, he acknowledged him as a dragon; though he withdrew from the world without regret, he ultimately attributed [his realization] to Heaven.
Only the Sage granted the principle of "frequent emptiness" exclusively to Yan Hui; yet he paired the exhaustion of the "two ends" with that of the vulgar man.
This, too, is a place where one cannot know the destination. Has the Master truly established his roots in the knowledge of how to dwell?
Below Shouchang, there was one named Jian Gong who personally received the evidence of transmission; he thus concealed himself in a place where no traces remain, not establishing a single thing.
Master Zi did not utter a single word for several decades. It was only because of a single word that coincided with the aspirations of Layman Hai-an that he revealed his true nature;
only then did it become known that he had seen the Master. When Master Lang returned to sweep the stupa of Shouchang, he joyfully offered to yield the Dharma seat to him.
Thus, I have ventured to compare him to Muzhou. Had Master Ling not met Layman Hai-an, then...
If you hang your mouth against the wall and do not encounter Master Lang, will you end up as nothing more than an incense burner in an ancient temple?

Such would surely not be the compassionate heart of one who seeks to save the world. Wherever Layman Hai-an went—whether at Boshan, Yingshan, Tiantong, or Jingshan—in every place he raised the banner of the Chan school. Yet, at the seat of Shouchang, there was Master Lang.
I consider this to be of great importance. That the new Dharma-sounds have spread so widely is entirely due to the power of you alone, Sir.

As I read your *Record of Pointing and Relying*, there is not a single word or phrase that does not possess the "killing blade" and the "life-giving sword," leaving people with no door for progress yet providing a place to turn their bodies.
The total function and great utility are all contained within this record; yet you remain serene and indifferent toward it. This is true dragon-like virtue.
[The text] was hidden. The Master [Zhang] held it fast in his breast. When the World-Honored One saw it, he must have recognized it silently.
I consider Master Chen’s interpretation to be words of true insight; I do not know what evidence Master Lang Haigan will provide.
When the turmoil of war reaches even to one’s bed and skin, before long I shall go to attend upon the two masters. Shall I take my rush shoes as travel funds? Bestowed.
The Duke [Li] composed this for a moment’s amusement.

Resident of Chu-Huang and Minister of the Ministry of Personnel in Beijing.
The upward path has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; where could the ancestral masters of successive generations even begin?
Yet, throughout all quarters, the discourse on Chan is vast and tumultuous, like thunder crashing and lightning flashing—all of which are merely gateways of expedient means, uttered out of necessity.
For this reason, Master Liang abandoned his post and entered the mountains, refusing to employ speech as a Buddhist activity, and instead practiced a different way.
There is no place to seek it elsewhere. I have long sought a master of the school in this day and age, and my heart has been won over by the great function of Master Shouchang Jian.
Regarding the story of Linji’s three blows of the staff, the Master revealed his original nature yet remained concealed; though the monastic communities repeatedly urged him to emerge, he would not.
Whenever there was even a single word or half-sentence, it was only after Duanduo respectfully entreated him that he would reveal it.
Nevertheless, he continued to keep it secret and did not transmit it lightly. The world yearned for its brilliance but was unable to behold it.
Thereupon, a disciple who had entered the inner circle recorded it in private and carved it for circulation; this was certainly not the Great Master’s original intention.

Within the record, the Great Master fully set forth the karmic conditions and pivotal moments regarding the Great Matter (mahā-vastu). Thus, prior to Shouchang, he finally bestowed his patched robe once more.
He entrusted it to him, yet the Master used it secretly and practiced it in concealment, appearing as if he were dull-witted and ignorant.

This is why those from all quarters submitted to his practice and realization as transcending the masses. People today, upon having even a slight insight, immediately think of thrusting their heads forward to show off;
hearing of the Great Master’s lofty style, they cannot help but feel a sudden sense of self-disappointment. Therefore, I have brought this forth to show it to those who are true masters of the craft.
On the Mid-Autumn Day of the Dingchou year of the Chongzhen era, his dharma younger brother Huang Duanduo respectfully inscribed this.

Addressing the assembly: If we discuss this matter, it is like the flight of a swift arrow; should one hesitate or deliberate, one will lose one's life.
To penetrate the profound is not to tread upon the long road to Chang’an; to transcend the ordinary is to walk with confident steps in every direction. Only Huanglong Peak is perverse:
he trusts neither the lips nor the tongue, but trusts only in awakening. What does he awaken to? "The head and horns of the Zhenzhou radish are revealed. *Du!* You must simply—
Only after vomiting it up can one attain it.

Addressing the assembly, he raised the example of the World-Honored One manifesting his twin feet at his parinirvāṇa. The Master said: "Neither extending nor non-extending, neither contracting nor non-contracting, and certainly not a donkey's head with horse's legs.
If someone were to say, 'It looks like a winter melon,' they would laugh themselves to death, collapsing within the Hall of the Empty King."

The Horn. Let us set aside the "laughing until one falls over" for now. As for this direct and precise phrase—how would you say it? [He snaps his fingers once and says: "Solid. Addressing the assembly:
"Eyeless and without nostrils, even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot fathom it. I, the old monk, open a single thread; it does not reside in words."
Regarding what was said: tell me, where is it? Is it in the center, or above and below, north, south, east, and west?
Although this is so, you must still see it directly for yourself once and for all.
Addressing the assembly: "The Zen of One Finger of Kūṭi—like a mute eating yellow myrobalan, it is difficult to bring forth the profound mystery in speech.

Shaking it out before gods and men, the void fills the seas, mountains, and rivers; hundreds of thousands of samādhis reside upon the tip of that finger. *Tu!* Do not speak erroneously before those with clear eyes."

Addressing the assembly: A dry dung pellet—seventeen hundred [cases] have all been leaked. The great chiliocosm is a vast expanse of heat; space is snapped in pieces, how many segments does it become?
Stepping out of the absurdity, one enters the tiger’s den. At the summer solstice there is bitter cold; at the winter solstice there is heat.
The tabby cat and the white ox have few who know them. Only Hanshan is permitted to laugh without end. *Du!* This too is like putting grit in the eye.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the dialogue concerning whether a dog has Buddha-nature or not. The Master said: "Old and decrepit as you are, your mouths have grown so accustomed to speaking.

At times the flames reach to the heavens; at other times the frost covers the earth. Even if you were to overturn the seas and mountains and topple Mount Sumeru, it would all be nothing more than a hollow display."
A lantern festival address to the assembly: This lantern has its mouth all over its body; when told to walk, it walks; when told to run, it runs.
Its appearances and disappearances are without cause; it hides its body within the Big Dipper. It confuses heaven and earth, making no distinction between before and after; above, it has no teacher.

There is no sequential transmission below; it continues the Buddha’s lamp of mind. Having fully penetrated through [the barrier], the public demonstration of picking up a flower cannot avoid falling into a conventional trap.
When the headless monk [Mahākāśyapa] broke into a smile, he revealed a stench. Once touched by even a little of this, it fills the universe and brings trouble upon one's descendants.
Its depths are profound and difficult to fathom. A single clap of thunder in a clear sky; a steel ox breaking its tether—truly without error.
Addressing the assembly, he held up his staff and said: "This staff is as alive as a dragon; its divine power and wondrous function manifest endlessly."
The body is not the four great elements; wisdom is endowed with the six supernormal powers. Being both ordinary and holy, one does not fall into partiality or the middle way.

Honored and revered by humans and devas, venerated by Buddhas and patriarchs—purely naked, starkly bare—the true wind of the eight directions and the numinous light are omnipresent and exceedingly lucid.
As for dwelling together with companions, people of this age do not encounter them. Striking once more, he said: "To follow tracks and seek footprints is entirely..."
There is nothing. When responding to circumstances as they arise, one must accord with public principle.
To the assembly: The sixteen-foot golden body is but a single blade of grass; when a monk cuts it off completely, it is just right.
Suddenly overturning it, the true mandate is carried out—how does this compare to pouring out a full wicker basket?

Nevertheless, this very state of being reckless has smashed through all the shifting nets. Alas! It is not that you have yet mounted the golden [lion].

He addressed the assembly: "A wooden wedge has no root or foundation; it lacks eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, yet it is able to stand head toward heaven and feet upon the earth."
The four quarters and eight directions are vast and level; for all Buddhas and sentient beings, there is no taboo. In a flash, one bumps into the red-bearded barbarian;
he overturns the azure heavens, leaving one gasping for breath. Gasping for breath! The tabby cat and the white ox laugh at this clumsy failure.
What are they laughing at? Their four legs reach toward the sky, yet they cannot crawl up.

Addressing the assembly: Arsenic is originally a blade for killing people; it requires a King of Physicians to handle it skillfully. Whether killing or bringing to life need not be called a "masterful hand";
only when one grasps the underlying pathology can one be considered eminent. Be careful and heed this.

Addressing the assembly: Those who first take up the Way must establish a firm and resolute will. Throughout the two-and-six periods of the day and night, you must wield the Ganjiang sword to subdue demons and spirits, severing the calamities of delusive emotions.
With the *huatou* held with constant intimacy, the light of the mind naturally arises; encompassing heaven and wrapping around the earth, it is fully manifest in every moment.
Only then can one be called a student of the Way, truly repaying the Dharma King. I exhort you, students: awaken to your native home. Reflect upon this!
Do not stop. Examine it again with great care. You must apply yourself with genuine investigation. To turn heaven and earth upside down is to stage a public demonstration.
This single matter of Zen practice is like hiding one's body within a fire; no matter how iron-hearted or copper-lunged they may be, they will surely be melted and transformed by it.
Nevertheless, even so, it is necessary for empty space to shatter and the great earth to sink level before there is...
The Path of Turning Back. At such a time, you would only just deserve to be struck with a staff. To the assembly:
Studying the Way through Zen meditation is fundamentally for the sake of the two words "birth and death," and not for any other matter. What is meant by "other matters"?
It is precisely where the mind stirs and thoughts arise in this present life; it is wherever there is conditioned action and effort, wherever there is grasping and rejecting.
To let go is it. To have cultivation and realization is it. To have purity and defilement is it. To have sages and ordinary people is it.
To have Buddhas and sentient beings is it. Even to compose odes and verses is it. To compose poetry and prose is it.
To discuss Chan and the Way is it. To discuss right and wrong is it. To discuss the past and the present is it.
Various ritual practices are not for the sake of the two characters "birth and death"; they are all merely other matters.

If you truly wish to address the two characters "birth and death," there is no need to seek them elsewhere; simply look toward the place where you put on clothes and eat food, and the place where you defecate and urinate.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at no place and for not even a hair’s breadth may you allow yourself to waver.
It is like a person who, upon seeing a fierce tiger, does nothing but hide their body and flee for their life. Or it is like a man entering the fray of battle;

his sole purpose is to slay the enemy leader, and he will not rest until the head is taken into his hands. What concern has he for gain or loss, purity or defilement, ordinary or holy, right or wrong? Otherwise, it is all in vain.
This is a mere waste of effort; when will we ever attain a time of true peace? If you practice in this manner, you may achieve a partial correspondence with the two words "birth and death.
Otherwise, it is all merely the performance of conditioned activities, which provides no benefit for the Way.
As the former Master said: "Do not be bound by minor gains; you must reach the ground of the ancients before you can resolve birth and death."
Freedom. Otherwise, it is entirely a matter of the shore of birth and death; truly, there will be no end to it.
Take care. Addressing the assembly: Those who practice Chan and study the Way must establish a firm and steadfast resolve and possess a great heart.
Ultimately, one must walk the same path as all Buddhas and sit upon the same seat as all Patriarchs. Only those who possess this mind may truly engage in Chan practice and study the Way.

Otherwise, having abandoned one’s parents and renounced affection, shaving one’s head and donning the black robes, one merely squanders the offerings of the faithful and brings shame upon the virtue of one’s teacher;
what benefit is there in this? To truly become a peer of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must [resolve] the two matters of life and death.
The character stands upright above the eyebrows, like one carrying a load of a thousand catties across a bamboo raft.
One cannot turn the head, blink the eyes, or shift the feet; the four limbs cannot move. There is only a single, alert mind intent on reaching the other shore.
To apply the mind in this manner may be called the practice of the beginner on the Way.
As for the Buddhas and patriarchs, as well as the very word "enlightenment," he had not yet touched upon them at all.

Addressing the assembly: A few fragments of white clouds fill the western ridges; a single wheel of red sun sets behind the eastern mountains.
It is like a donkey looking into a well, or the well looking at the donkey—very much like traveling back and forth between Ying and Bo.
But when it is raised in this manner, tell me: is it Mount Ying or Mount Bo? *Ei!* The setting glow and the solitary wild goose fly together; the autumn waters and the vast sky share one color.

Addressing the assembly: When the ancients established monasteries, they did so as a site for transforming the ordinary and forging the sage, and as a foundation for cultivating meditation and planting merit.

They sought to melt away the obstructions of accumulated habits and to polish the blindness of layered defilements. If these defilements are not cleansed, there is no way for the ground of the mind to become clear and penetrating;
if these habits are not eliminated, how can the source of Chan be thoroughly penetrated? It is not that they were unable to penetrate or clarify it; rather, they truly feared that...
This only serves to increase one's ignorance and obscuration. If you wish to attain purity and freedom from defilement, you must remain constantly correct at all times and ever fresh day by day.

Accomplish this practice with a single, continuous effort; do not say, "I will do it tomorrow" or "the day after. Arouse the mind that is inherently present and suddenly manifest the resolve that is already perfected.
There will come a day when, through direct encounter and impact, there is a sudden, thorough penetration—like the moon shining bright and the stars gleaming.
Only now do I begin to believe that what is manifest is not an error; only now do I realize that which was obscured by my ignorance.

This very reality remains vividly present, yet time passes swiftly and does not wait for man. If one does not attain clear penetration in this life, there will be another life, and yet another after that.
As a sutra says: "I and Śākyamuni Tathāgata were both ordinary beings together. Since the World-Honored One attained the Way, countless kalpas have passed."
[The Master] counts [the breaths]. Yet I am addicted to the six sense-objects and transmigrate through birth and death. How painful this is! How painful this is!

Addressing the assembly, he gave a shout and said, "Tell me, where does this one shout fall? After a long silence, he said, "It is easy for a sound to echo through an empty valley;
it is difficult to train the ear in a vacant hall."
Addressing the assembly in the hall: "O virtuous ones, beneath each of your own heels, you have been obscured regarding this great matter of your own nature for immeasurable kalpas.
If you do not attain clear realization in this life, there will be another life; yet whether there will be yet another birth thereafter is uncertain."
What kind of face is this? If you wish to clearly penetrate the Great Matter, do not follow the worldly current during these precious moments.

It is fortunate that you dwell within the precincts of the Dharma; cultivate both principle and practice together. Establish a resolute will and arouse a courageous mind. At all times, look after your own true master;
maintain this continuity from moment to moment without allowing it to wander. Should it suddenly wander, act with urgency.
Seek it out! Where was it lost? This single thought—whether once, twice, or thrice—it will naturally settle into stillness.
Do you believe this? Only by practicing will you know; overturn this one point and apply even greater diligence. It will become vivid and clear.
If you do not see the true Master, vow never to cease your resolve. Throughout the two-and-six periods of the day and night, remain like one playing a ball, staring wide-eyed.
Fixing your gaze with both eyes, attend to the incoming stimulus; even if various conditions of form and appearance arise, do not spare a glance for them.
If you apply your mind in this way for one month, two months, three months, or five months, yet do not personally see the true host, the ancients said:
"I will cut off the old monk's head and take it away! O virtuous ones, in this matter, neither spiritual sharpness nor clever intelligence matters; it concerns the beginner’s resolve.
In studying, one must seek a truly earnest and authentic investigation to achieve realization. Have you not seen how Master Xiangyan Zhixian first studied under Baizhang?

Was this merely your cleverness, your sharp intellectual understanding, and your conceptual consciousness? This is the realm of birth and death."

how could it be viewed as something trivial? Someone asked, "I have not yet seen the actual work of investigating Zen; I have only heard..."
Striking the bamboo, he attained enlightenment and said: "Had I not seen Master Guishan’s single question, I would have remained utterly bewildered.
Seeking even a single phrase with which to respond, I ultimately could find none. He then wept as he took his leave of Guishan; the effort required for further cultivation can be imagined.
Do you wish to see the true host? First, do not obscure your own nature. From immeasurable kalpas past, you have been blinded by distinctions of reality and unreality, gain and loss, right and wrong.
It is precisely for this reason that you are ignorant of the true master. Second, do not pretend to be a hero;

having acted as one who has accomplished his task, you follow your whims when encountering circumstances and let your mind run wild when meeting conditions, claiming that principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.
Such a "hero" is scrutinized by the Black-Faced Old Man. Third, do not seek out or memorize phrases from written records, preparing yourself to...

If one regards people as teachers and models, yet studies the Way in such a manner, wishing to clarify the great matter of the obscurity spanning immeasurable kalpas, one is far, far removed from it. Take care.
Addressing the assembly: You practitioners of Zen, do not merely discuss Zen; you must attain genuine realization before it will become perfect and complete.

Responding to circumstances and engaging with sentient beings, penetrating the profound mystery—all this lies in exhausting the fundamental source, not in mere verbal expression. Have you not seen it? What is Zen? It is like a monkey climbing a tree, tail and head hanging down together.
If one can thoroughly penetrate beyond heaven and earth, one will understand how to speak while remaining wordless. Practitioners of Zen, do not...

Studying Chan: what is valued is profound integrity and the firm establishment of one’s resolve. The ancient sages underwent this for thirty years; do not treat it as easy, for there is a timely opportunity.
Have you not seen? What is Chan? A lotus flower upon a rock, a spring within the fire. With a single sound from the *kiai* (the striking block), the whole body is manifested.
The void shatters and marrow fills the heavens. You who study Chan, do not wait for Chan. Seven times around the meditation cushion...
Half of it is missing. Sitting through the night with needle and awl, one has still not reached the end; only when the pillow falls to the ground does one begin to penetrate the mystery.
Have you not seen? What is Zen? It is like frying oil in a fierce flame. Once you have seen through the ancient message, grasping the clouds and riding the waves are all merely conditions.
You who study Zen, do not ask about Zen; you must know that upon reaching the shore, one is naturally at ease. Hold fast to the head-word.
This is not mere idle chatter. In the great and wondrous mountains, the *kai* (seal) of the separate transmission is realized.

Have you not seen it? What is Zen? Everyone washes their feet, climbs into bed, and sleeps. Suddenly, with the sound of a frog, heaven and earth grow narrow; singing and chanting to oneself, *li lo lan*.
Addressing the assembly: This very thing has no secret formula. I unfold my hidden treasure and speak it to you.
Even if one could explain it with full clarity, it would still be like a flake of snow flying from a red-hot furnace. As for the old monk speaking thus—does he have a secret formula or not?
After a long silence, he said: "Let us set aside the question of the Chan practitioner for a moment; what about the layperson? Although this is so, it is nevertheless not...

There is nothing to say. Have you not heard? "When three people travel together, there is bound to be someone who can serve as my teacher. If this is not yet the case, the discourse that follows is long;
it shall be entrusted for another day.
The Ancient Verse:

When the World-Honored One held up the flower, his governance reached ten thousand fathoms as he probed the deep abyss. Who would have thought the abyss was pierced through to its very bottom? Even if one encounters a golden-scaled dragon opening its mouth—
A laugh. The Yangtze River remains as ever, its waters reaching to the heavens.
To manifest the twin footprints is not a wondrous feat for drying up the vast ocean; to shatter Mount Sumeru is not a rare treasure. There is only the head of a dead cat that—suddenly!
Manifesting throughout the great trichiliocosm, his entire body is revealed.
Regarding the circumstances of childbirth, one passes through clouds and mist; another encounters water and makes his arrangements; three share a single nostril. Let him do as he will.
A barren woman conceives;
a seamless stupa plays on a swing within Lake Dongting. Only the blind turtle can see it all; flowers hang upside down upon the shadowless tree.
A shadow upon a beryl palace, with brocade spread over its tiles.

Seeking no sages and esteeming not one’s own spirit, one knows full well that this is to leap across the sea and play at the ends of the world. It is simply because the profound mystery has already shattered the household. Do not say that being "mindless" constitutes wondrousness.
The hand—mindless, it is still but a flower in the eye.
Deshan’s bowl:
without cause, he extends his almsbowl toward the human realm. Secretly testing while openly deceiving, he topples the banner pole. At the end, the secret transmission is truly remarkable.
How frightening! Who could have unraveled this chain of riddles in a donkey’s year?

The old woman who burned the hermitage lacked the eyesight of an elder; she could distinguish gold only by borrowing the discernment of a stone. To drive her out after she had burned the hut was truly extraordinary.
Who would have known that thorns would spring up everywhere upon the ground?

Zhaozhou’s “No-Character” (Wu) is like Mount Tai collapsing and crushing a gnat; breath ceases, the mind turns to ash, and the waves of consciousness flatten. This is not the single horn of a clay ox being revealed.
The eye—how could one know that the fierce tiger sits in the main hall?
Once returned, where does it go?
"The myriad dharmas return to One"—this too is groundless. "Seven catties heavy! How very coarse and crude! It is not coarse; let you look as you will.
The scale is in the stars, and the stars are in the pan—not in the pan. The golden crow leaps onto the jade balustrade.

Three catties of hemp, three catties of hemp—poverty to the very bone. The scale-weight falls to the ground, white as silver. Do you understand? Do not distinguish between the distant and the near. Yellow.
Beneath Longfeng, Jin Bin wears his cap;
the "Pine Tree Seed" has a boneless tongue universally acclaimed as supreme. Gathering all that is good and bad to compose this discourse-text: with one whole sound, heaven and earth [resound].
Black! The Persian swallows up the Iron Kunlun.

As for whether the dog has Buddha-nature or not—Venerable Zhaozhou, the ancient Buddha, is most rugged and steep. To touch its head is to lose its waist; only then does one see Nanquan called "The Myriad."
Fortune! His claws and fangs are bared alone, showing no mercy.

"Yunmen’s cake, Yunmen’s cake"—empty digging of a well. All the patch-robed monks under heaven merely paint shadows. To transcend Buddhas and surpass patriarchs is not yet enough to be called marvelous.
To treat a donkey as a horse—who would not command it?

For three days it emitted light, yet in the end it was nothing but gold given to the wealthy; where could one even speak of this tattered robe of the body? Last night at the third watch, the wheat was gathered.
Disciple, at daybreak you see nothing but the millstone being pushed in the millhouse.
Regarding Huanglong’s Three Barriers—the Buddha-hand and my own hand—you carry the cangue and wear the shackles. Speaking offhand, you have exposed your own shame.
My feet are like donkey’s feet; strictly avoid intellectual speculation. Stretching and contracting with total freedom, I trample the Five Peaks.
For those with the conditions for birth, there is no need for further proclamation. Even a hairless tiger knows how to act wild.
Question and Answer: Zen practitioner Dao Pu asked: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "To establish knowing and seeing within knowing and seeing is the root of ignorance;

when knowing and seeing are free from seeing, this is nirvāṇa. Regarding this, An of Rui鹿 (Ruilu) said: "To establish knowing within knowing and seeing is [ignorance]... [The text continues: "...is the root of ignorance."
The root of ignorance is the absence of knowing-seeing; seeing this is itself nirvana. My late teacher said: "The root of ignorance is the absence of knowing-seeing;
establishing knowing within knowing is itself nirvana. Regarding these two great elders, are their meanings the same as or different from the intent of the sutra?
Is there a distinction of superiority or inferiority between them, or not?
The verse in response: Three old fellows, truly strange and peculiar; with a single staff, they stir up the heavens.
Even with divine mechanisms and wondrous functions, how could excellence ever reach their limit?
Question: The *Avataṃsaka* takes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as its central tenet; what, then, is the central tenet of the Dharma-realm? Answer (in verse):
A single bright moon is reflected in a thousand rivers; In those thousand rivers, the bright moon is contained within a single orb.
When one penetrates the Flower Treasury World of Vairocana, The entire body manifests everywhere as the King of the Dharma.
Question: "While I was ill, Master Boshan previously pointed out: 'Leave the body behind, yet the body remains.
What is this remaining body? Answer (in verse):
"Since the beginningless arising of empty space, it has neither front nor back; One sees only the flickering lightning of empty space arise. Within and without are transparently luminous."
The One True Reality. Who can recognize this vision of the King of Emptiness?
Question: Are the external body and the existing body one or two? If you say they are two, logically they should not be two.
If you say they are one, why use the external one?
The verse in response: This old monk has never known calculation; he only knows how to abide in the state of just sufficiency. His application is unimpeded, a function beyond conventional measures;
to know its true essence is difficult to respond to or express.

Question: My late master spent his days from morning until evening setting down his chopsticks to wield his mattock, yet at night he would boast to himself that he had already reached the inner sanctum of Baizhang.
If one says, "If you do not work a day, you shall not eat a day," this still leaves one stranded halfway there.
Ultimately, where exactly is the inner sanctum of Baizhang?
The verse in response: The bridge of my nose twists with pain, yet I laugh "he-he. I alone regret that in the beginning, Old Bodhidharma Did not reach the intimate place of the fine mountain;
How else could he have leaped out from the mountain's cozy nest?
Question: The preface to the *New Mirror of Zen by Mount Bosan* states: "To speak the word 'Zen' within the Great Perfect Mirror is already to leave a scar.
I asked: "How much difference is there between the scar of speaking the word 'Zen' and the scar of speaking of the Great Perfect Mirror?
Mount Bosan said: "You have added yet another scar. If that is so, how should one understand the phrase "no scar"?
The Path.

Answer in verse: Originally there is no trace of things; how could there be the establishment of names and terms for "self" and "others"? With one shout, the records of a thousand ages are suddenly emptied;
what prevents the winds and dust from arising beyond the kalpas?
Question: An ancient worthy said, "When arising, it definitely arises; when departing, it truly does not depart. What is the meaning of this? Answer in verse:
Coming and going are without beginning; how wondrous is this matter! The mountain wind gently sends the white clouds home.
The golden crow and jade hare race east and west; How could light and darkness ever leave him behind?
Question: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. What is this place of non-abiding? Answer in verse:
The Way-person’s heart and gall are as vast as heaven; He goes straight to sleep within the Hall of the Empty King. When the Old King asks him, "Guest from where?
He turns his body, grasps his staff, and departs for West River.

Question: "The three minds are ultimately unattainable. Which one of these minds do you point to? When examined and scrutinized, is even that which cuts off the three periods of time worthy of receiving offerings?"
The verse in response: Three poor children share one family; there is no need for such bitter hardship to distinguish the dragon from the snake.
Even if one were to sit in stillness for incalculable eons, how could one ever avoid receiving offerings?
Question: It is fundamentally pure and serene; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Furthermore, tell me:
once these mountains, rivers, and the great earth have arisen, are they still fundamentally pure and serene?
The verse in response: That matter has never been lost to transmission from the outset; regardless of his formation or destruction, I do not shift.
Let the old barbarian go westward as he pleases; there remain three thousand [miles] where I cannot sleep at night.

Question: "A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; for three winters there is no warmth. The old woman burned the hut and drove him out, and throughout ancient and modern times, this has been praised and admired.
Thus we know both were masters of the Way. Yet, if one wishes to avoid falling into the hands of the woman who burns the hut, tell me:
how should this monk conduct himself?"
Answer in verse: A divine bow, once released, is as swift as the wind; what need is there to fear ten million layers of silver mountains?
Passing through them naturally brings forth joy and relief; yet burning the hermitage cannot avoid the futility of such labor.

The Emperor’s command is stern and majestic like the point of an arrow; How can there be room for deliberation or falling into partiality? The Seal of Orthodoxy is transmitted.

Question: I have heard that you, Master, had not yet entered the gate of the Sage of Confucius; yet, this very message was known to you upon first meeting the former Abbot.
Was it through diligent practice that you subsequently realized it?
Answer in verse: I recall when I first studied the Way in those days; the vast halls were left in utter desolation.
When my Master preached the Dharma like a rolling thunder, I, unworthy as I was, heard nothing but stamped my feet and beat my breast.
The layman Huang of Haigan asked, "When a person of good knowledge enters the gate and immediately discerns [others], what kind of eye do they possess?
The Master said, "Their heart does not betray others, and their countenance shows no shame."
Furthermore, he brought the sixteen questions posed by Chen Yunyi, the Provincial Education Commissioner, and requested the Master to provide responses.
Question: "A thirsty deer chases a mirage; how can it be made to rest? The Master said: "Wait until empty space falls to the ground, and then I shall tell you."
Question: "A mani jewel has been buried in dust for a long time; how can it be sought out so urgently? The Master said:
"Snow fills the red furnace. Question: "One strike, and everything is severed. How does one obtain such a sharp sword? The Master said: "Set aside the sharp sword for a moment;
bring me that which is already severed, and let the old monk examine it."
Question: "The taste of water is the same everywhere; yet there are those who rank it as the first spring and those who rank it as the second spring.
How do you distinguish between them? The Master said: "In my place, there is neither water nor taste."
Question: "In the middle of the night, one mistakes a thief for a son, or mistakes a son for a thief. How should this be judged? The Master said:
"Kill them both at once. Question:
"When one's own family members act as malevolent spirits, how should they be dealt with? The Master said: "Banish them to the Land of No-Birth."
Question: “How can one directly behold the true master? The Master said: “The pillar gives birth to a child.
Do you see it? Question:
“When the geomancer’s compass is moved back and forth, the needle always points south. Who is the master behind this? The Master said: “...”
The tethering stake for the donkey does not budge even when shaken.
[A student] asked, "A fine steed in a flash of lightning covers a thousand li in an instant; how can one overtake it in a single bound and take the reins in hand?
The Master said, "Great man, why would you follow a donkey in its tracks?"

Question: "Great Wisdom, you say to 'cut off the eight consciousnesses with one stroke. By what means do you establish yourself and find your livelihood? The Master said: "Seeing with the eyes as if blind. Question:
"Before a word is even spoken, why do you immediately strike or shout? The Master said: "Because the evil mind has not yet been eliminated."
Question: "When a Hu comes, a Hu appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears. Is this the substance of the mirror, or is it the light of the mirror? The Master said: "Three heads and six arms. Question:
"The sun rises and the moon sets; thunder roars and lightning flashes. The mountains are still and the clouds are leisurely; the water flows and the flowers bloom. Farmers sing and herdsmen [chant]."
[The Master] sang: "The wife and children play about; is there anything that is not this very thing bursting forth? How can one grasp it beneath the heels so that it may be used whenever needed?
The Master said: "When the talisman arrives, it is executed."
Question: "Nowadays, many practitioners fear the dark, vast expanse after death, yet they do not realize that the dark, vast expanse before their eyes is even more painful.
They often speak of impermanence and how great the matter of birth and death is, yet they do not realize that the moment-to-moment process of dying and being born right now is more urgent.
At this critical juncture, when facing the single blow of the heavy barrier, how does one apply oneself? The Master said: "The Great Bright Gate opens from—"

"Coming does not concern it. A question was asked: "Master Gao Feng said that one who has attained great penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death; why then is the life-root (mìnggēn) not severed?
If the life-root is not severed, how can one be called 'greatly penetrated'? What is it that they have penetrated? The Master said: "For now, present your life-root to me."
The Old Monk wrote this.
He was asked: "Regarding the single phrase that encompasses the eighty thousand gates and forever cuts off birth and death—how can such a phrase possess such power?
The Master said: "The 'Shang Daren' (The Elder Honorable One)—one should know the propriety of this."

A monk from Fuzhou asked, "What is it like to hold a hoe with empty hands? The Master said, "Only when the void is rotted away will you see the marrow. "What is it like to walk while riding a water buffalo?
The Master said, "The stone woman conceives and gives birth to a wooden child. "What is it like for a person to cross over a bridge?
The Master said, "Ten people fall in, nine and a half. "What is it like for the bridge to flow? The Master said, "The wooden man is carried away by the current."
"The water does not flow. The Master said, "A three-inch hempen rope passes through the flames.

Yipan asked, "How is it when face-to-face presentation occurs? The Master said, "Lingshan towers out beyond a thousand peaks. Yipan said, "How is it that facing each other yet being separated by a thousand mountains?
The Master said, "The waters of Dong River swirl as ten thousand streams are gathered. Yipan said, "The gatekeeper stands below..."
[Zhai] asked, "How do you respond? The Master said, "A precious sword brandished in the air clears the universe.
[Zhai] said, "As for that Precious Flower King’s Throne, who is it that ascends it? The Master said, "Ruler and minister in harmony: a hundred years of spring."
The Master of Verses asked the Householder Kaigan about the dialogue concerning the King of Emptiness. The householder replied, "A rotting winter melon," and subsequently presented him with a verse.

The patched-robed disciples of the Empty King [eat] rotting winter melons; they clearly behold the venerable master Huang Gong. Meeting the source from both left and right, he displays wondrous function:
where the cuckoo cries, the green willows lean.
To show Tu Yunchen, the lay practitioner:
when the mind is suddenly emptied, the whole body is manifested. What need is there to seek a Buddha further? The patriarchs have transmitted this without superfluous words;
it relies solely on secret resonance, free from all encumbrances.
To Chan master Shi Pu:
where there is no clarity is true clarity. To attain clarity through clarity is not yet the treasure.
Only after three days of deafness will you finally leap over the ancient pass and ford.
To the Chan practitioner Hongqiu:

Your backbone stands erect like an iron rod; your *huatou* is pure as ice and snow. Only when you overturn the raw, iron-like skin of your mother-birth will you finally leap over the pit of Buddhas and demons.
To the Chan practitioner Shidao Kun: Investigate the practice of *nianfo* by asking, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?
Who is the Buddha? Is it neither mind nor Buddha—what, then, is it? Master Ma did not have a kind heart;
he dug a three-foot pit right in the middle of level ground.

A Gift to My Dharma Nephew Huigao: I know your faith follows the singular style of your own house; Every sight you encounter returns entirely to the Palace of Great Enlightenment. The perfect radiance throughout kalpas is neither internal nor external;

The pure whiteness through many lifetimes has no center or periphery. Piercing mountains and penetrating seas, there is not a trace; Covering the earth and shielding the heavens—how could it be otherwise?
There are traces. Listen closely for the news of the fragrant breeze’s arrival; across the cavernous cliff, a single branch of red hangs suspended.

To the Zen practitioner Da-zong, this one phrase of the meditation topic is clear and distinct: it penetrates heaven and earth, leaving no trace of passage. If you do not encounter its ultimate radiance, you will remain lost.
Kung: "If you truly believe that the jewel in the robe is upon your own person, then show the Way to this Chan practitioner: 'The myriad dharmas return to the One;
the myriad dharmas are gathered back into the single One. When all Buddhas and sentient beings have together reached completion, what need is there for Qingzhou to spit out white [silk]?"
Saliva makes whatever it touches feel like glue or lacquer.

It shows that for a person of great capacity practicing Chan, right mindfulness continues uninterrupted and discursive thoughts do not arise. This "seed of the shadowless tree" must belong to one of great capacity.

Showing the Way: When a person of settled meditation contemplates the "cypress tree," they attain mastery over heaven and earth; only then do they know that which is new beyond the kalpas. Before the courtyard there is no cypress tree; within the limit there is the pupil of the eye.

At midnight, a tortoise gives birth to a white turtle.

As for principle: let his bones be exposed to the wind.

To show harmony to the Zen practitioner, a single phrase of the meditation topic is like the bright moon. When it is revealed throughout the entire body, who else could it be? Even if one were to suddenly emerge from Mahesvara himself—

requested by the scholar Zhang Jiusheng: To seek its origin is to ask no one; it is like a thorn stuck in the breast, or like cold ashes beyond expectation.
A turtle cannot escape from within a jar; a tortoise is easily caught in deep crags. When day breaks and the path is revealed, there is a clap of thunder across the level plain.
Sent to Layman Hai-an:

He replied: "Whether coming or not coming, whether going or not going—O Great Man, do not be reckless! It is a direct impact, not something forced; it is face-to-face."

To show the path: for Chan practitioner Huan, to attain life within life is not considered extraordinary; what is precious is the living pivot of one’s own transformative capacity. To revive after death is something that cannot be faked;

To the Zen practitioner Dalü, I give the name Jingyin:
his greatness is like space, his power is like the wind, his stillness leaves no trace, and his concealment leaves no mark. Such is this essential subtlety.

The official returned and invited various lay patrons (*upāsaka*) to request me to open the hall for formal preaching. I said, "My merit is slight and my wisdom shallow; I fear I would only bring disgrace upon our school."
The lay practitioners who protect the Dharma paid their respects and withdrew. In the tenth month of the Bingzi year, it was heard that the Great Master Juelang had arrived at Kuangshan;
they immediately dispatched messengers to welcome him back to Shouchang to preside over the Dharma seat of the late Master Xian and open the hall to preach the Dharma.
In the spring of the Dingchou year, he departed from the mountain carrying his staff and alms bowl, yet among the assembly there was not a single person who knew of it.

The Master left the mountains and went to Jianning in Min. After paying his respects at the pagoda of Master Bozan, he was subsequently invited by the Magistrate Huang Yuankong to return and serve as abbot. The Master resided at Shouchang for over twenty years in total.

Whatever monastic facilities were incomplete in the forest monasteries, the Master fully provided for them. In his later years, when Baofang Monastery was destroyed by fire, the Master rebuilt it once again.
He also restored Longhu Chan Monastery in his native district, completing it within a single year. The Master passed away in the Jichou year;
he was seventy-one years of age and had fifty years of seniority as a monk. He left behind one volume of recorded sayings. — By Grand Chancellor Li Mengbai.
